calibration.statement: The Pacific Ocean covers a greater surface area than all of Earth's land combined.
calibration.note: Pacific surface is about 165 million km2; total land is about 149 million km2.

calibration.statement: The summit of Mount Everest is the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre.
calibration.note: Chimborazo in Ecuador is farther out, because the Earth bulges at the equator.

calibration.statement: Alaska has more coastline than all other US states combined.
calibration.note: Alaska's tidal shoreline is roughly 54,000 km, more than the rest of the country together.

calibration.statement: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world.
calibration.note: About 9.2 million km2. Antarctica is a larger desert overall, but it is a cold one.

calibration.statement: Mount Kilimanjaro is located in Kenya.
calibration.note: It is in Tanzania, close to the Kenyan border.

calibration.statement: Reno, Nevada lies farther west than Los Angeles, California.
calibration.note: Reno is near 119.8 degrees west; Los Angeles is near 118.2 degrees west.

calibration.statement: Istanbul lies on two continents.
calibration.note: The Bosphorus divides its European and Asian sides.

calibration.statement: The whole of Africa lies within the Eastern Hemisphere.
calibration.note: The prime meridian crosses West Africa, so parts of Ghana, Mali and others sit west of it.

calibration.statement: Russia shares a land border with North Korea.
calibration.note: A short border of about 17 km along the Tumen River.

calibration.statement: The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest exposed land elevation on Earth.
calibration.note: More than 400 metres below sea level.

calibration.statement: Vatican City is the smallest sovereign state in the world by area.
calibration.note: About 0.49 km2.

calibration.statement: Iceland has a larger population than Malta.
calibration.note: Iceland is around 390,000 people; Malta is over 500,000 in a far smaller area.

calibration.statement: More people live in the Tokyo metropolitan area than in the whole of Australia.
calibration.note: Greater Tokyo is around 37 million; Australia is around 26 million.

calibration.statement: Australia is wider from east to west than the contiguous United States.
calibration.note: Australia spans roughly 4,000 km; the contiguous US spans roughly 4,300 km.

calibration.statement: Light takes more than one second to travel from the Moon to the Earth.
calibration.note: About 1.28 seconds at the mean distance.

calibration.statement: Venus is the hottest planet in the Solar System.
calibration.note: Surface near 465 C, hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun.

calibration.statement: A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.
calibration.note: It rotates in about 243 Earth days and orbits in about 225.

calibration.statement: Saturn is the only planet in the Solar System with a ring system.
calibration.note: Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune all have rings, they are simply much fainter.

calibration.statement: Helium was detected on the Sun before it was found on Earth.
calibration.note: Identified in the solar spectrum in 1868, isolated on Earth in 1895.

calibration.statement: Pure water is a good conductor of electricity.
calibration.note: Pure water is a poor conductor. Dissolved ions do the conducting in ordinary water.

calibration.statement: Sound travels faster through water than through air.
calibration.note: About 1,480 m/s in water against about 343 m/s in air.

calibration.statement: Window glass is a liquid that slowly flows at room temperature.
calibration.note: It is an amorphous solid. Old uneven panes come from the way they were made.

calibration.statement: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
calibration.note: Tall structures are struck repeatedly. The Empire State Building is hit many times a year.

calibration.statement: The Coriolis effect determines the direction water swirls when a household sink drains.
calibration.note: At that scale basin shape and initial motion dominate completely.

calibration.statement: Oxygen is the most abundant element by mass in the Earth's crust.
calibration.note: Roughly 46 percent, mostly locked in silicate and oxide minerals.

calibration.statement: Diamond is the hardest naturally occurring material known.
calibration.note: It sits at the top of the Mohs scale.

calibration.statement: Human beings normally have more than 23 pairs of chromosomes.
calibration.note: Exactly 23 pairs, 46 chromosomes in total.

calibration.statement: Bananas are measurably radioactive.
calibration.note: They contain potassium, and a fixed fraction of natural potassium is potassium-40.

calibration.statement: Bats are blind.
calibration.note: All bat species can see. Many also use echolocation.

calibration.statement: Sharks existed before trees did.
calibration.note: Sharks appear around 450 million years ago; the first trees around 390 million.

calibration.statement: An octopus has three hearts.
calibration.note: Two branchial hearts serve the gills and one systemic heart serves the body.

calibration.statement: Human blood is blue inside the body and turns red on contact with air.
calibration.note: Human blood is always red. Deoxygenated blood is a darker red.

calibration.statement: Goldfish have a memory span of only a few seconds.
calibration.note: They can be trained on tasks and retain them for months.

calibration.statement: Antibiotics are effective treatments for viral infections such as the common cold.
calibration.note: Antibiotics act on bacteria. They do nothing to viruses.

calibration.statement: A human body contains at least as many bacterial cells as human cells.
calibration.note: Current estimates put the ratio near one to one, slightly favouring bacteria.

calibration.statement: The human brain accounts for roughly a fifth of the body's resting energy use.
calibration.note: About 20 percent, from roughly 2 percent of body mass.

calibration.statement: Humans use only about ten percent of their brains.
calibration.note: Imaging shows activity throughout the brain. The claim has no basis.

calibration.statement: Bulls become enraged by the colour red.
calibration.note: Cattle are red-green colour blind. It is the movement of the cape that provokes them.

calibration.statement: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the first Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
calibration.note: The Great Pyramid is around 2560 BC; Cleopatra died in 30 BC; the landing was 1969.

calibration.statement: The Western Roman Empire fell before teaching began at Oxford.
calibration.note: 476 AD against evidence of teaching at Oxford from 1096.

calibration.statement: Harvard University was founded before calculus was developed.
calibration.note: Harvard was chartered in 1636; Newton and Leibniz worked in the 1660s to 1680s.

calibration.statement: A working fax machine was patented before the American Civil War began.
calibration.note: Alexander Bain patented an electric printing telegraph in 1843.

calibration.statement: Nintendo was founded before the Ottoman Empire ended.
calibration.note: Nintendo began in 1889 as a playing card maker; the Ottoman Empire ended in 1922.

calibration.statement: Anne Frank and Martin Luther King Jr. were born in the same year.
calibration.note: Both were born in 1929.

calibration.statement: Napoleon Bonaparte was unusually short for a Frenchman of his era.
calibration.note: He was about 1.68 m, close to average. The myth comes from differing inch measures and British caricature.

calibration.statement: The Hundred Years' War lasted more than one hundred years.
calibration.note: 1337 to 1453, about 116 years.

calibration.statement: Euro banknotes and coins entered circulation before the year 2000.
calibration.note: The euro existed electronically from 1999, but cash arrived in January 2002.

calibration.statement: The Great Wall of China is visible to the unaided eye from the Moon.
calibration.note: It is far too narrow. It is hard to pick out even from low Earth orbit.

calibration.statement: There are more distinct orderings of a standard 52-card deck than there are atoms in the observable universe.
calibration.note: 52 factorial is about 8 x 10^67. Atoms in the observable universe are about 10^80.

calibration.statement: A googol is larger than the number of atoms in the observable universe.
calibration.note: A googol is 10^100, against roughly 10^80 atoms.

calibration.statement: The number of possible chess games exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe.
calibration.note: The Shannon number is estimated near 10^120.

calibration.statement: The repeating decimal 0.999... is exactly equal to 1.
calibration.note: They are two notations for the same real number, provable several ways.

calibration.statement: It has been proven that every even number greater than two is the sum of two primes.
calibration.note: Goldbach's conjecture is verified far into the large numbers but remains unproven.

calibration.statement: There are infinitely many prime numbers.
calibration.note: Proved by Euclid.

calibration.statement: Pi has been proven to be irrational.
calibration.note: Lambert proved it in 1761.

calibration.statement: In the Monty Hall problem, switching doors wins two-thirds of the time.
calibration.note: Given the standard rules, switching wins whenever the first pick was wrong, which is two times in three.

calibration.statement: There are more atoms in a glass of water than there are glassfuls of water in all the Earth's oceans.
calibration.note: About 10^25 atoms in a glass, against roughly 10^22 glassfuls of ocean.

calibration.statement: The Amazon rainforest supplies about twenty percent of the world's oxygen.
calibration.note: A mature forest consumes nearly as much oxygen as it produces. Its net contribution is close to zero; most atmospheric oxygen came from ocean plankton over geological time.

calibration.statement: Sydney is the capital of Australia.
calibration.note: Canberra is, chosen as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

calibration.statement: Seen from space, the Sun appears yellow.
calibration.note: It is white. Atmospheric scattering removes blue light and makes it look yellow from the ground.

calibration.statement: Chameleons change colour mainly to blend in with their surroundings.
calibration.note: Colour change is driven mostly by temperature regulation and social signalling.

calibration.statement: A penny dropped from the top of the Empire State Building would kill a person it hit on the street.
calibration.note: Its terminal velocity is low and its shape unstable. It would sting.

calibration.statement: Viking warriors wore horned helmets in battle.
calibration.note: No horned helmet has been found in a Viking grave. The image comes from a 19th-century opera design.

calibration.statement: Albert Einstein failed mathematics as a schoolboy.
calibration.note: He had mastered calculus by fifteen. He did fail an entrance exam that covered non-scientific subjects.

calibration.statement: Different regions of the tongue are dedicated to detecting different basic tastes.
calibration.note: The tongue map came from a mistranslated 1901 paper. All taste types are detected across the tongue.

calibration.statement: Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Asia.
calibration.note: Fuji is about 3,776 m. Everest is about 8,849 m.

calibration.statement: Drinking alcohol raises the body's core temperature in cold conditions.
calibration.note: It dilates surface blood vessels, which feels warm while accelerating heat loss.

calibration.statement: A camel's hump stores water.
calibration.note: The hump stores fat, which is a reserve of energy.

calibration.statement: The Nobel Prizes include a category for mathematics.
calibration.note: There is no mathematics Nobel. The Fields Medal and Abel Prize fill that role.

calibration.statement: The official language of Brazil is Spanish.
calibration.note: It is Portuguese, a result of the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas.

calibration.statement: The Nile flows northward.
calibration.note: It rises near the equator and empties into the Mediterranean.

calibration.statement: Africa is the only continent lying in all four hemispheres.
calibration.note: The equator and the prime meridian both cross it.

calibration.statement: Greenland is larger than Australia.
calibration.note: Greenland is about 2.2 million km2; Australia is about 7.7 million. Map projections exaggerate Greenland.

calibration.statement: The Atacama is the driest non-polar desert on Earth.
calibration.note: Some weather stations there have never recorded rain.

calibration.statement: Lake Baikal holds more fresh water than any other lake.
calibration.note: Roughly a fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water, because it is extremely deep.

calibration.statement: The Mariana Trench is deeper than Mount Everest is tall.
calibration.note: About 10,900 m down against 8,849 m up.

calibration.statement: Mount Everest is getting taller.
calibration.note: The Indian plate is still colliding with Asia, lifting it a few millimetres a year.

calibration.statement: The Sahara was covered in grassland and lakes within the last ten thousand years.
calibration.note: The African Humid Period ended roughly 5,000 years ago.

calibration.statement: Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth.
calibration.note: A desert is defined by precipitation, not heat, and almost none falls there.

calibration.statement: Turkey is the only country that spans two continents.
calibration.note: Russia, Kazakhstan, Egypt, Georgia and others do too.

calibration.statement: The Dead Sea is a lake rather than a sea.
calibration.note: It is landlocked, fed by the Jordan, with no outlet.

calibration.statement: Norway shares a land border with Russia.
calibration.note: About 200 km in the far north.

calibration.statement: Mount Kilimanjaro has glaciers despite standing near the equator.
calibration.note: Altitude beats latitude, though they are retreating fast.

calibration.statement: Iceland has no native mosquitoes.
calibration.note: One of very few inhabited places on Earth where none are established.

calibration.statement: The Caspian Sea is the largest inland body of water on Earth.
calibration.note: About 371,000 km2, larger than Germany.

calibration.statement: Alaska is the easternmost state of the United States as well as the westernmost.
calibration.note: The Aleutian chain crosses the 180th meridian into the eastern hemisphere.

calibration.statement: Africa contains more countries than any other continent.
calibration.note: Fifty-four, against forty-four or so in Europe depending on the count.

calibration.statement: Bolivia has no coastline.
calibration.note: It lost its Pacific coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific.

calibration.statement: Switzerland has a short Mediterranean coastline.
calibration.note: It is entirely landlocked.

calibration.statement: The highest mountain in Europe is Mount Elbrus, not Mont Blanc.
calibration.note: Elbrus in Russia is 5,642 m; Mont Blanc is 4,808 m.

calibration.statement: The equator passes through Kenya.
calibration.note: It crosses the country a little north of Nairobi.

calibration.statement: A ship passing through the Panama Canal from the Atlantic to the Pacific travels east.
calibration.note: The isthmus curves, so the Pacific entrance sits southeast of the Atlantic one.

calibration.statement: The Rhine empties into the Mediterranean.
calibration.note: It flows into the North Sea through the Netherlands.

calibration.statement: The highest air temperature ever officially recorded on Earth was measured in Death Valley.
calibration.note: 56.7 C at Furnace Creek in 1913.

calibration.statement: Antarctica has no permanent human population.
calibration.note: Research staff rotate; nobody lives there indefinitely.

calibration.statement: The Sahara covers a greater area than the contiguous United States.
calibration.note: About 9.2 million km2 against 8.1 million.

calibration.statement: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt.
calibration.note: Around 200 Nubian pyramids, roughly double the Egyptian count, though they are smaller.

calibration.statement: The Andes form the longest continental mountain range on Earth.
calibration.note: About 7,000 km down the western edge of South America.

calibration.statement: There is a country entirely surrounded by South Africa.
calibration.note: Lesotho.

calibration.statement: New Zealand lies east of Australia.
calibration.note: Roughly 2,000 km across the Tasman Sea.

calibration.statement: Vatican City is entirely surrounded by Italy.
calibration.note: It sits inside Rome.

calibration.statement: The Amazon discharges more water than the next several largest rivers combined.
calibration.note: About a fifth of all river water reaching the oceans.

calibration.statement: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are all part of the United Kingdom.
calibration.note: The Republic of Ireland is not.

calibration.statement: Madagascar is the largest island in Africa.
calibration.note: Fourth largest in the world.

calibration.statement: Oslo is the capital of Sweden.
calibration.note: Oslo is Norway's capital. Sweden's is Stockholm.

calibration.statement: China borders more countries than any other nation.
calibration.note: China and Russia each border fourteen; neither is alone at the top.

calibration.statement: Mount Fuji is an active volcano.
calibration.note: It last erupted in 1707 and is still classified as active.

calibration.statement: Siberia makes up more than half of Russia's land area.
calibration.note: About three quarters of it, holding a small fraction of the population.

calibration.statement: The Tibetan Plateau is the highest and largest plateau in the world.
calibration.note: Averaging over 4,500 m, which is why it is called the roof of the world.

calibration.statement: The Suez Canal has no locks.
calibration.note: The Mediterranean and Red Sea are close enough in level that none are needed.

calibration.statement: Monaco is the second smallest country in the world.
calibration.note: After Vatican City, at about 2 km2.

calibration.statement: The Great Lakes hold about a fifth of the world's surface fresh water.
calibration.note: Roughly 21 percent.

calibration.statement: It is settled that the Nile is the longest river in the world.
calibration.note: Whether the Nile or the Amazon is longer depends on where you place the Amazon's source, and remains disputed.

calibration.statement: The Arctic is a continent.
calibration.note: It is ocean covered by sea ice. Antarctica is the continent.

calibration.statement: Istanbul is the capital of Turkey.
calibration.note: Ankara has been since 1923.

calibration.statement: The United States and Canada share the longest international land border in the world.
calibration.note: About 8,900 km including Alaska.

calibration.statement: The Hawaiian islands are still being formed by volcanic activity.
calibration.note: The Big Island is actively growing, and a new seamount is building offshore.

calibration.statement: Sea level is the same height everywhere on Earth.
calibration.note: Gravity, currents and winds make it vary by tens of metres.

calibration.statement: The Nile flows through Egypt alone.
calibration.note: It passes through eleven countries.

calibration.statement: The Himalayas are geologically young compared with the Appalachians.
calibration.note: Around 50 million years against several hundred million.

calibration.statement: Earth's seasons are caused by its distance from the Sun changing through the year.
calibration.note: They are caused by axial tilt. Earth is closest to the Sun in January.

calibration.statement: An astronaut exposed to space would freeze almost instantly.
calibration.note: A vacuum is a poor conductor. Heat is lost slowly by radiation; suffocation comes first.

calibration.statement: There is no gravity on the International Space Station.
calibration.note: Gravity there is about 90 percent of that at the surface. The station is in continuous free fall.

calibration.statement: The Sun produces energy by burning.
calibration.note: It fuses hydrogen into helium. Combustion would exhaust it in a few thousand years.

calibration.statement: Lightning travels only from cloud to ground.
calibration.note: Most lightning stays within or between clouds.

calibration.statement: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
calibration.note: It needs a medium to carry the pressure wave.

calibration.statement: Nothing carrying information can travel faster than light in a vacuum.
calibration.note: A cornerstone of relativity.

calibration.statement: Microwave ovens cook food from the inside out.
calibration.note: They heat the outer centimetre or two directly; the rest warms by conduction.

calibration.statement: Gold is denser than lead.
calibration.note: About 19.3 against 11.3 grams per cubic centimetre.

calibration.statement: Water expands when it freezes.
calibration.note: Which is why ice floats and pipes burst.

calibration.statement: Glass can be recycled indefinitely without losing quality.
calibration.note: Unlike paper or most plastics.

calibration.statement: Under some conditions hot water can freeze faster than cold water.
calibration.note: The Mpemba effect. It is real but the mechanism is still argued over.

calibration.statement: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and therefore the hottest.
calibration.note: It is closest, but Venus is hotter because of its atmosphere.

calibration.statement: One side of the Moon never receives sunlight.
calibration.note: The far side gets as much sunlight as the near side. It is never visible from Earth, which is a different thing.

calibration.statement: Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet.
calibration.note: Reclassified in 2006 because it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood.

calibration.statement: Jupiter is more massive than all the other planets combined.
calibration.note: By roughly a factor of two and a half.

calibration.statement: Stars twinkle because of turbulence in Earth's atmosphere.
calibration.note: Seen from space they do not twinkle.

calibration.statement: A black hole would pull in objects that a star of the same mass would not.
calibration.note: Its gravity at a given distance depends only on mass. Replace the Sun with an equal-mass black hole and the orbits are unchanged.

calibration.statement: Diamonds form from coal.
calibration.note: Almost all natural diamonds predate land plants entirely.

calibration.statement: Helium is a finite resource on Earth that escapes to space once released.
calibration.note: It is light enough to leave the atmosphere permanently.

calibration.statement: Silver conducts electricity better than copper.
calibration.note: Silver is the best conductor of any metal; copper is used because it is far cheaper.

calibration.statement: Absolute zero has never been reached.
calibration.note: Laboratories have come within billionths of a degree, but it cannot be reached.

calibration.statement: Uranium occurs naturally in ordinary rock and seawater.
calibration.note: In small concentrations almost everywhere.

calibration.statement: Iron cannot rust without both oxygen and water.
calibration.note: Which is why it does not rust in dry air or in oxygen-free water.

calibration.statement: Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon.
calibration.note: Usually under 2 percent carbon.

calibration.statement: A lightning bolt is hotter than the surface of the Sun.
calibration.note: Around 30,000 K against roughly 5,800 K.

calibration.statement: Metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature because it conducts heat away from your hand faster.
calibration.note: Your skin senses heat flow, not temperature.

calibration.statement: Pencil leads contain lead.
calibration.note: They are graphite and clay. The name is a historical mistake.

calibration.statement: An atom is mostly empty space.
calibration.note: The nucleus holds nearly all the mass in a tiny fraction of the volume.

calibration.statement: Spent nuclear fuel glows green.
calibration.note: Cherenkov radiation in a cooling pool is blue, and unshielded fuel does not glow visibly.

calibration.statement: Radio waves are a form of light.
calibration.note: Both are electromagnetic radiation; they differ only in wavelength.

calibration.statement: Crude oil formed mainly from dinosaurs.
calibration.note: Mostly from marine plankton and algae.

calibration.statement: Tides are caused by the Moon alone.
calibration.note: The Sun contributes roughly half as much; the two align at spring tides.

calibration.statement: The Earth is slightly wider across the equator than pole to pole.
calibration.note: About 43 km wider, because it is spinning.

calibration.statement: The Sun emits more green light than any other single wavelength.
calibration.note: Its peak output is in the green, though the mix reads as white.

calibration.statement: Titanium is stronger than steel by weight.
calibration.note: Its strength-to-density ratio is higher, though many steels are stronger in absolute terms.

calibration.statement: A superconductor that works at room temperature and normal pressure has been confirmed.
calibration.note: Several claims have been made and none have survived replication.

calibration.statement: Neutrinos pass through the entire Earth almost without interacting.
calibration.note: Trillions pass through you every second.

calibration.statement: A vacuum pulls objects towards it.
calibration.note: There is nothing there to pull. Surrounding pressure pushes them in.

calibration.statement: Plasma is the most common state of ordinary matter in the universe.
calibration.note: Stars are plasma, and stars hold most of the visible matter.

calibration.statement: Aircraft can navigate without any external signal using inertial guidance.
calibration.note: Accelerometers and gyroscopes track motion from a known start point.

calibration.statement: The half-life of a radioactive isotope can be changed by heating it.
calibration.note: It is essentially fixed, unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemistry.

calibration.statement: Individual electrons move through a wire at close to the speed of light.
calibration.note: They drift at millimetres per second. The signal travels fast, not the electrons.

calibration.statement: Oxygen itself burns.
calibration.note: It does not burn. It is the oxidiser that lets other things burn.

calibration.statement: Antimatter has been produced in laboratories.
calibration.note: Antiprotons and even anti-hydrogen atoms have been made and trapped.

calibration.statement: Distilled water is a poorer conductor of electricity than tap water.
calibration.note: Tap water carries dissolved ions; distilled water does not.

calibration.statement: The Moon is moving away from the Earth.
calibration.note: About 3.8 cm a year, measured by laser ranging.

calibration.statement: GPS satellites must correct for relativistic effects to stay accurate.
calibration.note: Without it, positions would drift by kilometres a day.

calibration.statement: Sound travels faster in warm air than in cold air.
calibration.note: Speed rises with temperature.

calibration.statement: A rainbow is actually a full circle.
calibration.note: The ground cuts off the lower half; from an aircraft you can see the whole ring.

calibration.statement: The Earth's magnetic north pole is, in magnetic terms, a south pole.
calibration.note: Opposite poles attract, which is why a compass needle's north end points there.

calibration.statement: Alcohol boils at a lower temperature than water.
calibration.note: Ethanol boils at about 78 C.

calibration.statement: Helium raises the pitch of your voice.
calibration.note: It does not change pitch. It changes the resonance of the vocal tract, altering timbre.

calibration.statement: You can estimate a storm's distance in kilometres by dividing the seconds between flash and thunder by three.
calibration.note: Sound covers roughly a kilometre every three seconds.

calibration.statement: Fingernails and hair keep growing after death.
calibration.note: The skin retracts as it dehydrates, which makes them look longer.

calibration.statement: Taste buds are replaced roughly every two weeks.
calibration.note: They regenerate continuously through life.

calibration.statement: The liver can regrow after a large part of it is removed.
calibration.note: The only human internal organ with that capacity.

calibration.statement: The appendix is now thought to have a function.
calibration.note: Evidence points to a reservoir of gut bacteria and a role in immunity.

calibration.statement: The average person swallows several spiders a year while asleep.
calibration.note: Invented as an example of a claim people repeat without checking. There is no evidence for it.

calibration.statement: The tongue is the strongest muscle in the human body.
calibration.note: It is not a single muscle and is not the strongest by any standard measure.

calibration.statement: Sharks must keep swimming or they die.
calibration.note: Some species must, but many can pump water over their gills while resting.

calibration.statement: Elephants cannot jump.
calibration.note: Their leg structure and weight make it impossible.

calibration.statement: Octopus blood is blue.
calibration.note: It uses copper-based haemocyanin rather than iron-based haemoglobin.

calibration.statement: A cockroach can survive for a time without its head.
calibration.note: It breathes through body openings and dies of thirst rather than instantly.

calibration.statement: Honey does not spoil.
calibration.note: Edible honey has been recovered from ancient tombs.

calibration.statement: No penguin species lives in the Arctic.
calibration.note: All wild penguins live in the southern hemisphere.

calibration.statement: Botanically, a banana is a berry.
calibration.note: A strawberry is not.

calibration.statement: A peanut is not a nut.
calibration.note: It is a legume, related to peas and beans.

calibration.statement: Eating carrots improves night vision beyond correcting a deficiency.
calibration.note: A wartime propaganda story. Vitamin A prevents deficiency; excess does not sharpen sight.

calibration.statement: Sugar makes children hyperactive.
calibration.note: Controlled trials find no effect. Parents' expectations shape what they report seeing.

calibration.statement: Cracking your knuckles causes arthritis.
calibration.note: Long-term studies find no association.

calibration.statement: Being cold and wet causes the common cold.
calibration.note: Colds are caused by viruses. Cold weather correlates because people crowd indoors.

calibration.statement: Vaccines cause autism.
calibration.note: The original claim was fraudulent and retracted; very large studies find no link.

calibration.statement: Healthy kidneys and a healthy liver remove waste without help from detox products.
calibration.note: That is their function.

calibration.statement: There is strong evidence that everyone needs eight glasses of water a day.
calibration.note: The figure has no solid basis; needs vary and food supplies much of it.

calibration.statement: Adults grow no new brain cells at all.
calibration.note: Neurogenesis occurs at least in the hippocampus, though the extent is debated.

calibration.statement: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker.
calibration.note: The blunt cut end feels coarser. Growth rate and thickness are unchanged.

calibration.statement: Dogs see only in black and white.
calibration.note: They are dichromats: they see blues and yellows but confuse reds and greens.

calibration.statement: Fish can feel pain.
calibration.note: They have nociceptors and show behavioural responses consistent with pain.

calibration.statement: Science cannot explain how bumblebees fly.
calibration.note: It was explained decades ago. The old claim came from applying fixed-wing aerodynamics to a flapping wing.

calibration.statement: Every cell in your body contains the same DNA.
calibration.note: Red blood cells have no nucleus, and immune cells rearrange their DNA.

calibration.statement: There is more genetic variation within human populations than between them.
calibration.note: A long-standing and repeatedly confirmed finding.

calibration.statement: A tomato is botanically a fruit.
calibration.note: It develops from the flower's ovary and contains seeds.

calibration.statement: Some mammals lay eggs.
calibration.note: Monotremes: the platypus and echidnas.

calibration.statement: Whales are fish.
calibration.note: They are mammals: warm-blooded, air-breathing, and they nurse their young.

calibration.statement: Spiders are insects.
calibration.note: They are arachnids: eight legs, two body segments, no antennae.

calibration.statement: Bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics within a single human lifetime.
calibration.note: Resistance has emerged within years of a drug's introduction.

calibration.statement: People with type O negative blood are universal donors of red cells.
calibration.note: Their red cells carry neither A, B nor Rh D antigens.

calibration.statement: A person can live a normal life without a spleen.
calibration.note: With a raised risk of certain infections, managed by vaccination.

calibration.statement: The human heart sits in the centre of the chest, tilted to the left.
calibration.note: It is roughly central, not on the left side as usually drawn.

calibration.statement: The two human lungs are not the same size.
calibration.note: The left is smaller, to make room for the heart.

calibration.statement: Babies are born with more bones than adults have.
calibration.note: About 300, many of which fuse into the adult 206.

calibration.statement: Stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve metal.
calibration.note: It can corrode some metals; the stomach lining is replaced constantly to survive it.

calibration.statement: Goosebumps are a leftover reflex from having more body hair.
calibration.note: The muscle raises hairs to trap air or look larger. It does little on bare skin.

calibration.statement: Yawning is contagious in humans and in some other species.
calibration.note: Observed in chimpanzees and dogs too.

calibration.statement: Humans can distinguish more than five basic tastes.
calibration.note: Umami joined the classic four, and evidence for fat as a sixth is growing.

calibration.statement: Mosquitoes kill more humans each year than any other animal.
calibration.note: Through malaria, dengue and other diseases they carry.

calibration.statement: Counting tree rings gives a reliable age for most temperate trees.
calibration.note: One ring per growing season, which also records climate.

calibration.statement: Plants consume oxygen as well as producing it.
calibration.note: They respire continuously; in daylight photosynthesis outpaces it.

calibration.statement: Cancer is a single disease.
calibration.note: It is a large family of diseases with different causes, behaviour and treatment.

calibration.statement: Placebos can produce measurable physiological effects.
calibration.note: Particularly for pain and nausea, though they do not shrink tumours.

calibration.statement: The human gut contains hundreds of millions of neurons.
calibration.note: The enteric nervous system, sometimes called the second brain.

calibration.statement: Losing sleep measurably weakens the immune response.
calibration.note: Shown in vaccination and infection studies.

calibration.statement: Individual organisms evolve during their lifetime.
calibration.note: Populations evolve across generations. Individuals develop; they do not evolve.

calibration.statement: In evolutionary terms, fitness means reproductive success rather than strength.
calibration.note: An organism that survives but never reproduces has zero fitness.

calibration.statement: Humans share the majority of their DNA with chimpanzees.
calibration.note: Around 98 to 99 percent depending on how it is counted.

calibration.statement: Two blue-eyed parents can have a brown-eyed child.
calibration.note: Eye colour involves several genes, so it is uncommon but possible.

calibration.statement: A person can be struck by lightning more than once.
calibration.note: One US park ranger was struck seven times.

calibration.statement: Educated Europeans in Columbus's day believed the Earth was flat.
calibration.note: Its roundness had been accepted since antiquity. The dispute was over its size.

calibration.statement: Europeans reached North America before Columbus.
calibration.note: Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows is dated to around 1000 AD.

calibration.statement: Marie Antoinette said 'let them eat cake'.
calibration.note: The line appears in Rousseau before she arrived in France.

calibration.statement: Nero played the fiddle while Rome burned.
calibration.note: The fiddle did not exist. He was reportedly not even in Rome when the fire started.

calibration.statement: Napoleon's troops shot the nose off the Sphinx.
calibration.note: Drawings made before his campaign already show it missing.

calibration.statement: Those convicted in the Salem witch trials were burned at the stake.
calibration.note: They were hanged. One was pressed to death.

calibration.statement: Einstein won his Nobel Prize for relativity.
calibration.note: It was awarded for the photoelectric effect.

calibration.statement: Magellan completed the first circumnavigation of the globe.
calibration.note: He was killed in the Philippines. His crew finished the voyage.

calibration.statement: The Great Wall of China is one continuous wall.
calibration.note: It is many walls built by different dynasties, with gaps and parallel sections.

calibration.statement: The pyramids were built by slaves.
calibration.note: Evidence points to paid labourers who were housed, fed and buried nearby with honour.

calibration.statement: Medieval people typically died in their thirties.
calibration.note: Average lifespan was dragged down by infant mortality. Those reaching adulthood often lived into their sixties.

calibration.statement: Romans built vomitoria as rooms for vomiting during feasts.
calibration.note: A vomitorium is a passage that empties an amphitheatre of its crowd.

calibration.statement: The iron maiden was a medieval torture device.
calibration.note: It was assembled in the eighteenth century from unrelated pieces and presented as medieval.

calibration.statement: Chastity belts were widely used by crusading knights.
calibration.note: Almost all surviving examples are later curiosities or fakes.

calibration.statement: The Emancipation Proclamation freed all slaves in the United States.
calibration.note: It applied only to states in rebellion. The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery.

calibration.statement: Hitler was elected chancellor by a majority of German voters.
calibration.note: He was appointed chancellor; the Nazis never won a free majority.

calibration.statement: The First World War began after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand.
calibration.note: In Sarajevo in June 1914.

calibration.statement: The Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
calibration.note: In November of that year.

calibration.statement: The first Moon landing took place in 1969.
calibration.note: Apollo 11, July 1969.

calibration.statement: Printing with movable type was invented in Europe.
calibration.note: It appeared in China centuries earlier. Gutenberg's press was independent and mechanised.

calibration.statement: Paper was invented in China.
calibration.note: Around the second century AD.

calibration.statement: Gunpowder was invented in China.
calibration.note: By alchemists seeking an elixir of life.

calibration.statement: So-called Arabic numerals originated in India.
calibration.note: They reached Europe through Arabic scholarship, which is why the name stuck.

calibration.statement: The Library of Alexandria was destroyed in a single fire.
calibration.note: It declined over centuries through several episodes of damage and neglect.

calibration.statement: The Hundred Years' War was fought continuously.
calibration.note: It was a series of conflicts with long truces between them.

calibration.statement: Magna Carta established democracy in England.
calibration.note: It constrained the king in favour of barons. Its democratic reading came much later.

calibration.statement: The guillotine was invented in France.
calibration.note: Similar beheading machines were used earlier in Scotland, Ireland and Italy.

calibration.statement: The Black Death is now agreed to have spread only through rat fleas.
calibration.note: Human ectoparasites and person-to-person transmission are increasingly thought to explain its speed.

calibration.statement: The 1918 influenza pandemic began in Spain.
calibration.note: Spain reported it freely as a neutral country, so the name stuck. Its origin is uncertain.

calibration.statement: Cleopatra was ethnically Greek rather than Egyptian.
calibration.note: She came from the Ptolemaic dynasty founded by one of Alexander's generals.

calibration.statement: Alexander the Great never lost a major battle.
calibration.note: He died at thirty-two having been undefeated in pitched battle.

calibration.statement: The Roman Empire ended in 476 AD.
calibration.note: The western half did. The eastern empire continued until 1453.

calibration.statement: The Declaration of Independence was signed on 4 July 1776.
calibration.note: It was adopted that day; most delegates signed in August.

calibration.statement: The Boston Tea Party was a protest against a tax increase on tea.
calibration.note: The Tea Act lowered the price. The objection was to the principle of the tax and the monopoly.

calibration.statement: Britain abolished the slave trade before it abolished slavery itself.
calibration.note: The trade in 1807, slavery in the empire in 1833.

calibration.statement: New Zealand was the first self-governing country to give women the vote.
The Titanic's builders officially advertised it as unsinkable.
calibration.note: The claim was press language and hindsight, not an official slogan.

calibration.statement: The Second World War in Europe ended before the war in the Pacific.
calibration.note: May 1945 against September 1945.

calibration.statement: Churchill was prime minister for the whole of the Second World War.
calibration.note: Chamberlain held office until May 1940, and Churchill lost the 1945 election before Japan surrendered.

calibration.statement: The United States and the Soviet Union never fought each other directly in a declared war.
calibration.note: They fought through proxies instead.

calibration.statement: The Apollo guidance computer had less processing power than a modern phone.
calibration.note: By an enormous margin.

calibration.statement: The internet grew out of a military research network.
calibration.note: ARPANET, funded by the US Department of Defense.

calibration.statement: The World Wide Web and the internet are the same thing.
calibration.note: The web is one service running on the internet, invented around twenty years later.

calibration.statement: The Y2K problem was a hoax that required no real work.
calibration.note: Enormous remediation effort preceded it, which is part of why little went wrong.

calibration.statement: Galileo dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to test gravity.
calibration.note: The story comes from a biographer. He argued the case with inclined planes and reasoning.

calibration.statement: Newton was struck on the head by a falling apple.
calibration.note: He described watching one fall. The blow to the head is embellishment.

calibration.statement: Darwin published his theory immediately after the Beagle voyage.
calibration.note: He waited about twenty years, publishing only when Wallace reached the same conclusion.

calibration.statement: Mozart died penniless and was buried in a pauper's grave.
calibration.note: He earned well and had a conventional middle-class burial for the time.

calibration.statement: Van Gogh sold only one painting in his lifetime.
calibration.note: Long repeated, but he sold and traded several works.

calibration.statement: Shakespeare invented every word first attested in his plays.
calibration.note: He is the first surviving record for many, which is not the same as inventing them.

calibration.statement: The Bastille held only a handful of prisoners when it was stormed.
calibration.note: Seven.

calibration.statement: The Mayflower pilgrims sought religious freedom for everyone.
calibration.note: They sought freedom to practise their own faith, and did not extend it to others.

calibration.statement: A United States president can win office without winning the popular vote.
calibration.note: It has happened five times.

calibration.statement: The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
calibration.note: In December of that year.

calibration.statement: The Great Pyramid was the tallest structure made by humans for thousands of years.
calibration.note: It held that record for about 3,800 years.

calibration.statement: One is a prime number.
calibration.note: A prime has exactly two distinct divisors. One has a single divisor.

calibration.statement: Zero is an even number.
calibration.note: It is divisible by two with no remainder.

calibration.statement: All infinite sets are the same size.
calibration.note: The reals are strictly larger than the integers, as Cantor proved.

calibration.statement: The mean and the median of a data set are always close together.
calibration.note: A single extreme value can move the mean far from the median.

calibration.statement: A 50 percent fall followed by a 50 percent rise returns you to where you started.
calibration.note: 100 falls to 50, then rises to 75. Percentage changes do not cancel.

calibration.statement: After a fair coin lands heads ten times, tails becomes more likely on the next toss.
calibration.note: The coin has no memory. It stays even.

calibration.statement: In a room of 23 people, there is better than an even chance two share a birthday.
calibration.note: About 50.7 percent, because it counts pairs rather than matches to one person.

calibration.statement: A strong correlation between two variables establishes that one causes the other.
calibration.note: A third factor, reverse causation or chance can all produce it.

calibration.statement: An exceptional result is likely to be followed by a more ordinary one, even with no intervention.
calibration.note: Regression to the mean, and it fools people into crediting the intervention.

calibration.statement: A small sample is more likely than a large one to produce an extreme average.
calibration.note: The law of small numbers. Small hospitals report both the highest and lowest rates.

calibration.statement: A p-value of 0.05 means there is a 95 percent chance the hypothesis is true.
calibration.note: It is the probability of data this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. Quite different.

calibration.statement: Parallel lines never meet in any geometry.
calibration.note: On a sphere every pair of great circles intersects.

calibration.statement: The decimal expansion of pi eventually repeats.
calibration.note: It is irrational, so it never repeats.

calibration.statement: No real number squared gives a negative result.
calibration.note: Which is why the imaginary unit was introduced.

calibration.statement: The sum of the first n odd numbers is always a perfect square.
calibration.note: 1, 4, 9, 16 and so on.

calibration.statement: In the Monty Hall problem it makes no difference whether you switch.
calibration.note: Switching wins two times in three under the standard rules.

calibration.statement: A treatment can appear better in every subgroup yet worse overall.
calibration.note: Simpson's paradox, which comes from unequal group sizes.

calibration.statement: Truly random data tends to look more clustered than people expect.
calibration.note: People asked to fake randomness spread points out too evenly.

calibration.statement: Choosing 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 in a lottery is less likely to win than a scattered set.
calibration.note: Every combination is equally likely. It would just be shared with more people.

calibration.statement: A test that is 99 percent accurate gives a 99 percent chance of disease when positive.
calibration.note: That depends on how common the disease is. With a rare condition, most positives are false.

calibration.statement: Folding a sheet of paper fifty times would make it thick enough to reach beyond the Moon.
calibration.note: Doubling fifty times gives an absurd figure, though the fold is physically impossible.

calibration.statement: Almost everyone has more than the average number of arms.
calibration.note: A few people have fewer than two, which drags the mean below two.

calibration.statement: Armour should be added where returning aircraft show the most bullet holes.
calibration.note: Wald's insight: those are the survivable hits. Armour belongs where survivors were not hit.

calibration.statement: A wider confidence interval indicates greater certainty.
calibration.note: It indicates less. Precision narrows the interval.

calibration.statement: When a measure becomes a target it tends to stop being a good measure.
calibration.note: Goodhart's law.

calibration.statement: Inuit languages have hundreds of unrelated words for snow.
calibration.note: They are polysynthetic, so they build compounds. The count is not remarkable.

calibration.statement: English has more native speakers than any other language.
calibration.note: Mandarin Chinese and Spanish both have more native speakers.

calibration.statement: Latin has no native speakers today.
calibration.note: It survives liturgically and academically, and evolved into the Romance languages.

calibration.statement: Every sentence in English requires a verb.
calibration.note: Even one-word imperatives such as 'Go' contain one.

calibration.statement: Double negatives were once standard in English.
calibration.note: They were standard for centuries. Chaucer and Shakespeare both use them for emphasis.

calibration.statement: The rule against splitting infinitives was borrowed from Latin grammar.
calibration.note: Latin infinitives are single words and cannot be split, so the rule never applied to English.

calibration.statement: The order of the alphabet has a logical basis.
calibration.note: It is inherited from Phoenician with no systematic principle behind the sequence.

calibration.statement: Some people speak Esperanto as a native language.
calibration.note: A small number raised in it from birth.

calibration.statement: Sign language is universal.
calibration.note: There are hundreds of distinct sign languages, mutually unintelligible.

calibration.statement: Chinese is written with an alphabet.
calibration.note: It uses logographic characters representing morphemes, not an alphabet.

calibration.statement: GDP measures a country's wellbeing.
calibration.note: It measures output. It counts a disaster's cleanup as growth and ignores unpaid work.

calibration.statement: Zero inflation means no prices are changing.
calibration.note: It means the basket average is flat. Individual prices still move in both directions.

calibration.statement: Economists agree that raising the minimum wage always reduces employment.
calibration.note: The empirical literature is genuinely divided, which is unusual for a textbook prediction.

calibration.statement: A trade deficit is the same thing as national debt.
calibration.note: One is a flow between countries, the other money owed by a government.

calibration.statement: Printing money always causes immediate inflation.
calibration.note: It depends on demand, capacity and expectations. Japan expanded its money supply for years with little inflation.

calibration.statement: Money already spent and unrecoverable should not affect the decision about what to do next.
calibration.note: The sunk cost fallacy is failing to ignore it.

calibration.statement: The cost of a choice includes the best alternative given up.
calibration.note: Opportunity cost.

calibration.statement: At 7 percent annual growth, money roughly doubles in ten years.
calibration.note: The rule of 72 gives about 10.3 years.

calibration.statement: Earning enough to enter a higher tax bracket can reduce your take-home pay.
calibration.note: Only income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate.

calibration.statement: Insurance is a bad deal on average for the buyer.
calibration.note: It must be, or insurers would not exist. People buy it to avoid ruin, not to gain.

calibration.statement: A market price reflects the value of a good to everyone who buys it.
calibration.note: It reflects the value to the marginal buyer. Everyone else values it at least that much.

calibration.statement: Automation has historically caused permanent mass unemployment.
calibration.note: It has destroyed particular jobs and created others. The transition costs are real and fall unevenly.

calibration.statement: Global population growth is now slowing.
calibration.note: Fertility has fallen sharply almost everywhere; the debate is about when the peak comes.

calibration.statement: The share of the world living in extreme poverty has fallen sharply since 1990.
calibration.note: One of the largest changes of the period, and widely misperceived.

calibration.statement: Private browsing mode hides your activity from your internet provider.
calibration.note: It only stops the browser storing it locally. The network still sees the traffic.

calibration.statement: Deleting a file removes its contents from the disk immediately.
calibration.note: It normally unlinks the entry. The data stays until overwritten.

calibration.statement: Apple computers cannot get malware.
calibration.note: They are targeted less, not immune.

calibration.statement: More megapixels always means a better photograph.
calibration.note: Sensor size, lens quality and processing usually matter more.

calibration.statement: Charging a modern phone overnight destroys the battery.
calibration.note: Charge controllers stop at full. Heat and time at high charge matter more.

calibration.statement: A fridge magnet will erase a modern phone or credit card chip.
calibration.note: Chips and flash memory are unaffected. Old magnetic stripes were vulnerable.

calibration.statement: Quantum computers are simply faster at everything than ordinary computers.
calibration.note: They offer speedups for a narrow class of problems and are worse at most tasks.

calibration.statement: A password's length matters more than its mixture of symbols.
calibration.note: Length increases the search space far faster than character variety.

calibration.statement: A VPN makes you anonymous online.
calibration.note: It moves trust to the VPN provider, which can still see and log your traffic.

calibration.statement: Software whose source code is public is inherently less secure.
calibration.note: Visibility allows review. Security by obscurity is not considered sound.

calibration.statement: Bats are the only mammals capable of true sustained flight.
calibration.note: Others glide; only bats fly.

calibration.statement: Hair grows faster in summer than in winter.
calibration.note: Modestly, with warmth and circulation.

calibration.statement: Owls can rotate their heads a full 360 degrees.
calibration.note: About 270 degrees, which is remarkable but not a full turn.

calibration.statement: Ostriches bury their heads in the sand when frightened.
calibration.note: They lower their heads to the ground, which looks like burying from a distance.

calibration.statement: Lemmings periodically throw themselves off cliffs in mass suicides.
calibration.note: A myth cemented by a 1958 Disney documentary that staged the scene.

calibration.statement: Touching a baby bird makes its mother reject it.
calibration.note: Most birds have a poor sense of smell and will not abandon a chick.

calibration.statement: Daddy longlegs are the most venomous spiders but cannot bite humans.
calibration.note: Neither half is true, and one common daddy longlegs is not a spider at all.

calibration.statement: One dog year equals exactly seven human years.
calibration.note: A rough rule at best. Dogs mature very fast early and the ratio varies hugely by breed.

calibration.statement: Human blood is filtered by the kidneys many times a day.
calibration.note: The entire volume passes through roughly every half hour.

calibration.statement: All birds migrate.
calibration.note: Many species are year-round residents.

calibration.statement: Identical twins have identical fingerprints.
calibration.note: They share DNA but fingerprints form partly at random in the womb.

calibration.statement: Alligators and crocodiles are the same animal.
calibration.note: Different families, distinguishable by snout shape and tooth arrangement.

calibration.statement: Taking large doses of vitamin C prevents colds in the general population.
calibration.note: Trials show at most a small reduction in duration, not prevention.

calibration.statement: A person can donate a kidney and live normally.
calibration.note: The remaining kidney compensates.

calibration.statement: The Earth's inner core is solid despite being hotter than the outer core.
calibration.note: Immense pressure keeps it solid.

calibration.statement: A compass points to true north.
calibration.note: It points to magnetic north, which moves and differs from true north by a varying angle.

calibration.statement: Rubber tyres protect a car's occupants from lightning.
calibration.note: The metal shell conducts the charge around them. The tyres are irrelevant.

calibration.statement: Microwave ovens make food radioactive.
calibration.note: They use non-ionising radiation, which cannot induce radioactivity.

calibration.statement: Explosions in space make no sound to a nearby observer.
calibration.note: There is no medium to carry it.

calibration.statement: When it is summer in Europe it is winter in Australia.
calibration.note: Opposite hemispheres, opposite tilt towards the Sun.

calibration.statement: Aluminium was once more valuable than gold.
calibration.note: Before cheap smelting, it was a precious metal. The Washington Monument is capped with it.

calibration.statement: Air temperature always falls with altitude.
calibration.note: Temperature inversions reverse it, and the stratosphere warms with height.

calibration.statement: Modern lithium-ion batteries need to be fully discharged to avoid a memory effect.
calibration.note: That affected older nickel-cadmium cells. Full discharges shorten lithium-ion life.

calibration.statement: There is a temperature at which the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales read the same.
calibration.note: Minus 40.

calibration.statement: Continents move at roughly the speed fingernails grow.
calibration.note: A few centimetres a year.

calibration.statement: There is gold dissolved in seawater.
calibration.note: In concentrations far too low to extract profitably.

calibration.statement: The Wright brothers were the first people to fly in any aircraft.
calibration.note: Balloons and gliders carried people long before. They achieved the first powered, controlled, sustained flight.

calibration.statement: Some Roman concrete structures have lasted two thousand years.
calibration.note: Seawater concrete in particular grows stronger over time.

calibration.statement: Universities are a medieval European invention with no earlier parallels.
calibration.note: Institutions of higher learning existed earlier elsewhere, including al-Qarawiyyin in Fez.

calibration.statement: Julius Caesar was the first Roman emperor.
calibration.note: He was dictator. Augustus was the first emperor.

calibration.statement: The oldest continuously operating companies in the world are more than a thousand years old.
calibration.note: Several Japanese firms, including a hotel founded in the eighth century.

calibration.statement: British forces burned the White House during the War of 1812.
The French Revolution and the American Revolution overlapped in time.
calibration.note: The American ended in 1783; the French began in 1789.

calibration.statement: SOS was chosen because it stands for Save Our Souls.
calibration.note: It was chosen for its simple, unmistakable Morse pattern. The phrase came afterwards.

calibration.statement: Women could vote in some US states before the national amendment passed.
calibration.note: Wyoming from 1869, decades before 1920.

calibration.statement: Ada Lovelace is credited with writing the first published algorithm intended for a machine.
calibration.note: For Babbage's Analytical Engine.

calibration.statement: Prohibition in the United States made drinking alcohol illegal.
calibration.note: It banned manufacture, sale and transport. Drinking and possession were not federally banned.

calibration.statement: Everest was first summited in the 1950s.
calibration.note: By Hillary and Tenzing in 1953.

calibration.statement: Britain used a non-decimal currency within living memory.
calibration.note: Pounds, shillings and pence until 1971.

calibration.statement: Ten percent of 40 is the same as 40 percent of 10.
calibration.note: Both are four. Percentages commute.

calibration.statement: Odds of 3 to 1 against mean a probability of one third.
calibration.note: They mean one in four, or 25 percent.

calibration.statement: Half of all drivers are below the median in driving skill by definition.
calibration.note: That is what a median is, which is why most people rating themselves above it cannot all be right.

calibration.statement: Two dice are more likely to total 7 than any other number.
calibration.note: Six of the thirty-six combinations give seven.

calibration.statement: The product of two negative numbers is negative.
calibration.note: It is positive.

calibration.statement: A fraction with a larger denominator is always smaller.
calibration.note: Only if the numerators match. Three quarters exceeds one half.

calibration.statement: Most real-world data follows a normal distribution.
calibration.note: Income, city size and word frequency are all heavily skewed.

calibration.statement: Compound interest grows a sum in a straight line.
calibration.note: It grows exponentially, which is why intuition underestimates it badly.

calibration.statement: Past investment performance reliably predicts future returns.
calibration.note: Which is why the warning is legally required.

calibration.statement: Holding many different assets reduces risk without necessarily reducing expected return.
calibration.note: The central result behind diversification.

calibration.statement: Deleting an app removes all the data a company holds about you.
calibration.note: It removes the local copy. Server-side records remain until deleted at the source.

calibration.statement: Clearing cookies prevents all online tracking.
calibration.note: Device fingerprinting and account logins persist across cookie clears.

calibration.statement: Signal bars indicate connection speed.
calibration.note: They indicate signal strength. A strong signal on a congested tower can still be slow.

calibration.statement: End-to-end encryption means the service provider cannot read the message contents.
calibration.note: That is what distinguishes it from encryption in transit.

fermi.prompt: How many piano tuners work in Chicago?
reference: Chicago metro population: about 9 million, so roughly 3 million households.
Say 1 household in 50 owns a piano: about 60,000 household pianos.
Add institutional pianos in schools, churches, bars and halls: call it 10,000 more, so 70,000.
A piano in use gets tuned about once a year: 70,000 tunings a year.
A tuner does 3 to 4 a day, so 800 to 1,000 a year with travel.
70,000 / 900 is roughly 80 full-time tuners.
fermi.answer: About 80 to 200. Trade directories list a few hundred, many of them part time.

fermi.prompt: How many times does a human heart beat in an average lifetime?
reference: Resting rate is about 70 per minute; average 75 across the day to allow for activity.
75 x 60 = 4,500 per hour.
4,500 x 24 = about 108,000 per day.
108,000 x 365 = about 39 million per year.
At 75 years: 39 million x 75 = about 3 billion.
fermi.answer: Roughly 2.5 to 3 billion. Most mammals land within a factor of a few of 1 billion.

fermi.prompt: How many breaths does a person take in a lifetime?
reference: Resting respiration is about 14 per minute; call the daily average 16.
16 x 60 x 24 = about 23,000 breaths per day.
23,000 x 365 = about 8.4 million per year.
Over 75 years: 8.4 million x 75 = about 630 million.
Childhood rates are higher, which nudges the figure up.

fermi.prompt: How many golf balls fit inside a standard school bus?
reference: Bus interior: about 12 m long, 2.4 m wide, 2 m tall = 58 cubic metres.
Subtract seats, wheel wells and engine housing: call the usable space 50 cubic metres.
A golf ball is 4.27 cm across, so its own volume is about 4.1 x 10^-5 cubic metres.
Random packing of spheres fills about 64 percent of space, so each ball claims 6.4 x 10^-5 cubic metres.
fermi.answer: Roughly 500,000 to 900,000. The packing fraction is the step most people forget.

fermi.prompt: How many cells are there in the human body?
reference: Do not average over cell types: one type dominates the count.
Red blood cells run about 5 million per microlitre of blood.
Blood volume is about 5 litres, which is 5 million microlitres.
5 x 10^6 x 5 x 10^6 = 2.5 x 10^13 red blood cells alone.
Red cells are roughly 80 percent of all cells by number, so the total is around 3 x 10^13.
Cross-check by mass: 70 kg at about 1 nanogram per generic cell would give 7 x 10^13, the same order.

fermi.prompt: How many hairs are on a typical human head?
reference: The haired scalp is roughly a cap 30 cm across, so about 700 square centimetres.
Follicle density on the scalp is about 150 to 200 per square centimetre.
fermi.answer: Roughly 100,000 to 150,000. Blond hair runs denser and finer, red hair sparser and thicker.

fermi.prompt: How many grains of sand are on all the beaches of Earth?
reference: A medium grain is about 0.5 mm across, so about 6 x 10^-11 cubic metres; allow for packing gaps and call it 10^-10 cubic metres each.
That gives about 10^10 grains per cubic metre of sand.
World coastline is roughly 350,000 km; say a fifth of it is sandy beach, so 70,000 km, or 7 x 10^7 metres.
Take a beach cross-section 50 m wide and 5 m deep: 250 square metres.
Volume = 7 x 10^7 x 250 = 1.75 x 10^10 cubic metres.
fermi.answer: Around 10^19 to 10^20. Fewer than the stars in the observable universe, which is the usual point of the comparison.

fermi.prompt: How many trees are there on Earth?
reference: Global forest area is about 4 billion hectares, which is 4 x 10^13 square metres.
Tree density in forest varies widely; take 500 stems per hectare as a middling figure.
4 x 10^9 hectares x 500 = 2 x 10^12 trees in forests.
Add savanna, orchards, parks and street trees: call it half again.
Total around 3 x 10^12.
fermi.answer: About 3 trillion. The 2015 Crowther survey put it at 3.04 trillion, which surprised people by being far higher than earlier guesses.

fermi.prompt: How many seconds have elapsed since the year 1 AD?
reference: Elapsed years: about 2,025.
Seconds in a year: 365.25 x 24 x 3,600 = about 3.16 x 10^7.
A useful thing to memorise: pi x 10^7 seconds is close to one year.

fermi.prompt: How much does a typical fair-weather cumulus cloud weigh?
reference: Take a cumulus roughly 1 km on each side: 10^9 cubic metres.
Liquid water content in such a cloud is about 0.5 grams per cubic metre.
10^9 x 0.5 g = 5 x 10^8 grams = 5 x 10^5 kilograms.
That is around 500 tonnes of water, held up by rising air.
fermi.answer: About 500,000 kg. The mass is real; the droplets are just too small to fall fast.

fermi.prompt: What is the total length of all the blood vessels in one human body?
reference: Capillaries dominate the total length; arteries and veins are negligible by comparison.
Estimates of capillary count run from 10^10 to 10^11.
Each capillary is roughly 0.5 to 1 mm long.
Take 4 x 10^10 capillaries at 1 mm: 4 x 10^7 metres = 40,000 km.
The commonly quoted 100,000 km figure assumes a capillary count near 10^11.
fermi.answer: Order of 10^4 to 10^5 km. Enough to wrap the equator at least once.

fermi.prompt: How many pizzas are sold in the United States in one year?
reference: US population is about 335 million.
Say the average person eats pizza once every two weeks: 26 servings a year.
One pizza feeds about three people, so 335 million x 26 / 3 = about 2.9 billion pizzas.
Cross-check from the other side: the US pizza industry turns over roughly 46 billion dollars at maybe 15 dollars a pizza, which is about 3 billion.
Two independent routes agreeing is the strongest signal a Fermi estimate can give you.

fermi.prompt: How many litres of petrol do passenger cars in the United States burn in a year?
reference: Light vehicles in regular use: about 250 million.
Average annual distance: about 19,000 km, which is 12,000 miles.
Fuel economy averages about 10 litres per 100 km, which is roughly 24 miles per gallon.
fermi.answer: About 5 x 10^11 litres, or roughly 130 billion US gallons.

fermi.prompt: How many words does a person speak in a lifetime?
reference: Recording studies put daily speech at about 16,000 words for both men and women.
16,000 x 365 = about 5.8 million words a year.
Assume 72 years of talking after early childhood.
fermi.answer: Around 400 million. The often-repeated claim that women speak three times as many words as men did not survive measurement.

fermi.prompt: How many windows are there in New York City?
reference: NYC has about 3.5 million housing units.
A typical apartment has about 5 windows: 17.5 million residential windows.
Commercial, institutional and industrial buildings add perhaps another 50 percent.
Total around 25 to 30 million.
The classic interview trap here is to start from the population instead of from housing units.

fermi.prompt: How many individual ants are alive on Earth right now?
reference: Earth's land area is about 1.3 x 10^14 square metres.
Much of it is desert, ice or bare rock; call the ant-supporting area 10^14 square metres.
Ground surveys find on the order of 100 ants per square metre in productive habitat, far fewer elsewhere.
Take a weighted average near 150 per square metre over the supporting area.
fermi.answer: About 2 x 10^16, or 20 quadrillion. Their combined mass is comparable to that of all wild birds and mammals together.

fermi.prompt: How much energy is released by a single lightning bolt, in joules?
reference: Charge transferred in a typical flash is about 5 coulombs.
The potential difference between cloud and ground is on the order of 10^8 volts.
Energy = charge x voltage = 5 x 10^8 joules.
Cross-check: that is about 140 kilowatt-hours, roughly what a house uses in a week.
fermi.answer: Order of 10^9 joules. Most of it leaves as heat, light and sound, not as usable electricity.
